Aura  AI:  An  Agentic  Hybrid  Graph-Vector 
 RAG  Framework  for  Privacy-Preserving 
 Document Intelligence 
 DR.  DEEPIKA  SIRMORIA¹,  PENDRU  RINITH  REDDY²,  NYTHIK  REDDY³,  CHARAN 
 TEJA⁴ VARUN KUMAR  5

 ABSTRACT 
 Enterprise  level  documents  are  growing  faster  than  many  tools  which  are  being  used  to 
 query  them.Cloud-based  tools  are  scalable  but  leads  to  a  trouble  in  maintaining  data 
 residency  and  might  charge  an  unpredictable  cost.And  also  they  are  dependent  on  external 
 API's.Here  Aura  AI  is  locally  deployed  RAG  which  pairs  with  ChromaDB  vector  retrieval 
 and  with  a  NetworkX  knowledge  graph.The  vector  ones  handle  the  semantic  similarity  and 
 the  graph  ones  handle  the  entity  level  reasoning.If  the  retrieved  content  comes  back  thin,  an 
 agent  named  Langgraph,is  used  to  rewrite  the  query  and  the  updated  one  is  sent  to  the 
 model.The  whole  stack  runs  on  Llama3(8B  Parameters)  via  an  open-source  tool 
 Ollama-which  eliminates  API  Calls,and  ensures  data  residency.When  tested  on  50  queries 
 across  12  documents,the  model  scored  0.7698  on  RAGAS  Metrics  which  are  BERTSCORE 
 F1  at  0.8909,Answer  Relevance  at  0.8566  which  are  far  ahead  of  the  previous  approaches 
 like  RAG,GraphRAG.Here  a,  Fast  API  backend  is  used  to  handle  real-time  interaction  and 
 data ingestion. 
 Keywords:  Retrieval-Augmented Generation • Knowledge  Graph • Agentic AI • LangGraph • 
 ChromaDB • Llama 3 • Hybrid Retrieval • Local Inference 
 INTRODUCTION 
 Background and Motivation 
 As  an  impact  of  LLMs  [10],  typical  information 
 retrieval  systems  were  designed  differently.  They 
 also  tell  lies,  lack  access  to  proprietary  or  up  to 
 date  documents,  and  do  not  provide  the  source  of 
 an  answer  [16].  That  is  edge  in  enterprise 
 anywhere  accuracy  and  sourcing  are  audit  able 
 that ain't 
 This  is  exactly  what  RAG  was  designed  to  solve 
 [1].  Step  2:  Embedding  your  query, 
 cross-referencing  it  against  an  indexed  corpus, 
 bolting  on  top  n  answers  to  prompt  It  works,  to  a 
 point.  But  it  can:  not  reason  across  entity 
 relations;  not  recover  if  the  first  retrival  pass 
 comes  back  wrong,  and  do  perform  without 
 sending  data  to  a  cloud  API.  Before  anything  else 
 is  even  on  the  table  to  be  discussed,  that  last  one 
 does  in  many  enterprise  use  cases.These  two 
 failure  modes  are  likely  to  compound  on  each 
 other.  If  retrieval  messes  up  on  a  query,  there  is  no 
 fallback  and  rather  then  having  the  model  to  say. 
 Nobody  catches  it,  except  it's  main  users  for  the 
 first time. 
 Literature Review 
 In  early  2020,RAG  was  introduced  by  Lewis  et  al. 
 [1]  and  most  research  work  done  on  it,treated  it  as 
 a  retrieval  problem,but  Karpukhin  et  al.[2] 
 depicted  that  bi-encoder  models  like  DPR  are 
 very  helpful  for  open-domain  QA.But 
 DPR,doesn't  reason  the  documents,but  only 
 retrieves  them.Guu  et  al.[3]  worked  on 
 REALM,which  bought  retrieval  and  pre-training 
 rather  adding  it  at  the  end.This  helps  in  making 
 the  knowledge  better  at  ground  level  with 
 whatever corpus existed during training. 
 The  next  thing  goes  on  how  things  happen  after 
 retrieval  in  which  Izacard  and  Grave[4]  split  the 
 passage  encoding  and  decodings  in  FiD,which 
 helped  in  synthesizing  the  answers  across  various 
 documents,  through  this  requires  special 
 fine-tuning.  Shi  et  al.  [5]  kept  the  language  model 
 entirely  hands-off  in  REPLUG,  aggregating 
 across  passages  at  the  probability  level  clean  in 
 theory,  but  it  needs  token-level  access  that  local 
 inference  setups  rarely  expose.  Ma  et  al.  [6]  made 
 the  case  for  rewriting  queries  before  retrieval, 
 which  helps.  The  problem  is  the  rewrite  is 
 static.Asai  and  colleagues  published  a  paper  in 
 August  2023  called  "Self  -  RAG.  "  They  fine  - 
 tuned  an  LLM  with  a  series  of  tokens  to  serve  as 
 signals,  these  tokens  reflect  upon  the  content 
 being  written  to  indicate  the  need  for  retrieved 
 content  and  whether  that  content  actually  aids  the 
 generation  process.  Self  -  RAG  obtained  a 
 BERTScore  of  0.8312,  but  this  process  required 
 instruction  fine  -  tuning  of  the  underlying  model. 
 Most  people  with  a  PC  likely  wouldn't  have 
 access  to  enough  GPUs  to  perform  the  task.  Edge 
 and  colleagues  wrote  the  paper  "GraphRAG,  "  a 
 method  for  query  -  summarization  by 
 summarizing  communities  hierarchically  to  create 
 "super  -  communities"  when  answering  dataset  - 
 level  questions,  than  questions  concerning  local 
 text.  Graphrag  scored  0.8578  BERTScore, 
 whereas  Self  -  RAG  scored  0.8312,  but  since 
 graphrag  was  "not  designed  for  answering 
 questions that were at a local level". 
 Research Gap 
 We  note  a  progression  in  two  dimensions:  that's, 
 in  the  quality  of  retrieval  and  context  grading  and 
 in  the  third  dimension:  structure  in 
 reasoning.Unfortunately,  no  published  system 
 combines  in  a  single  model  hybrid  retrieval 
 (vector  and  graph),  agent  self  -  correction  guided 
 by  context  grading  and  local,  all  on  device 
 deployment.Previous  works  improved  dense 
 retrieval  quality,  while  more  recent  ones  gained 
 multi  -  passage  summarization.Later  research 
 added  agentic  feedback,  prompt  reforming  and 
 finally  GraphRAG  gave  insight  into  the  structural 
 knowledge present in entity nodes. 
 Problem Definition 
 A  key  need  for  the  system:  document  intelligence 
 that  can  find:  (1)  based  on  similarities  in  text  (e. 
 g.  ,  question  Q  and  document  d1  similarity)  AND 
 semantic  relations  (e.  g.  ,  "CEO  of  Google  is 
 Larry  Page"),  (2)  autonomously  self  -  correct  by 
 agent  context  grading  and  rephrasing  the  question. 
 (3)  Runs  on  the  local  machine  only  without  losing 
 out  on  quality.  Formally,  for  query  Q  and  corpus 
 D,  produce  answer  A  so  that  A  is  factually 
 accurate,  matches  Q  on  meaning  and  A  doesn't 
 get  sent  anywhere  outside  of  the  machine  where 
 D lives. 
 Objectives/Contributions 
 The primary contributions of this work are: 
 ●  A  hybrid  retrieval  layer  combining 
 ChromaDB  vector  search  and  NetworkX 
 graph  traversal,  hitting  Precision@5  of 
 0.8234  better  than  any  single-method 
 model tested till date. 
 ●  A  LangGraph  agent  that  grades  retrieved 
 context  and  rewrites  queries  when  they 
 fall  thin,  scoring  0.7256  on  Rewrite 
 Robustness  the  highest  across  all 
 evaluated systems. 
 ●  A  fully  local  deployment  on  Llama  3  via 
 Ollama,  removing  cloud  API 
 dependencies  without  hurting 
 retrieval,generation  quality  and  also 
 saving credits. 
 ●  An  evaluation  against  eight  RAG 
 baselines  on  a  50-question  benchmark, 
 evaluated  on  the  basis  of  six  metrics, 
 with  a  composite  RAGAS  score  of 
 0.7698. 
 RELATED WORK 
 Classical Retrieval-Augmented Generation 
 Approaches 
 Lewis  et  al.  [1]  built  the  first  real  RAG  pipeline: 
 DPR  retrieval  feeding  into  a  BART  generator.  The 
 encoder  maps  queries  and  passages  into  a  shared 
 embedding  space  and  pulls  the  top-k  results  by 
 inner  product  similarity.  One  retrieval  pass,  then 
 generate.  If  the  retrieved  passages  were  bad, 
 there's  no  fallback  —  the  system  doesn't  know 
 and  doesn't  check.  BERTScore  F1  of  0.7312, 
 Answer Relevance of 0.6524. 
 Karpukhin  et  al.  [2]  focused  specifically  on  the 
 retrieval  side.  DPR  trains  separate  BERT  encoders 
 for  questions  and  passages  using  in-batch 
 negatives,  which  outperforms  sparse  BM25 
 retrieval.  BERTScore  F1  of  0.7489.  But  it's  still  a 
 static  retrieval  step  —  no  reformulation,  no 
 second  attempt,  no  correction  if  the  first  pull 
 misses. 
 REALM  which  was  used  by  Guu  et  al.  [3]  in 
 which  he  combined  the  retrieval  and  pre-training 
 into  a  single  approach  which  gave  a  result  of 
 0.7623  which  is  the  BERTScore  F1.  The  problem 
 is  rigidity.  The  corpus  is  fixed  at  pre-training 
 time,  so  updating  it  means  retraining,  which  is 
 expensive.  And  once  it  retrieves,  it  just  generates. 
 No  iteration,  no  self-correction,  nothing 
 resembling agency. 
 Recent Deep Learning and Advanced Methods 
 Izacard  and  Grave  [4]  fixed  one  specific  thing: 
 early  RAG  threw  all  retrieved  passages  into  a 
 single  context  window  and  hoped  the  model 
 sorted  it  out.  FiD  encodes  each  passage  separately 
 alongside  the  query,  then  fuses  them  in  the 
 decoder.  Multi-passage  synthesis  got  better  — 
 BERTScore  F1  of  0.7801.  What  didn't  change:  the 
 system  still  can't  tell  if  the  retrieved  passages 
 were worth retrieving. It encodes whatever it gets. 
 Shi  et  al.  [5]  tried  a  different  fix  with  REPLUG  — 
 ensemble  the  generation  probabilities  across 
 retrieved  documents  instead  of  touching  the 
 retrieval  mechanism  at  all.  BERTScore  F1  of 
 0.8012,  a  real  improvement  in  factual  accuracy. 
 The  problem  is  that  bad  retrieval  just  gets 
 ensembled.  REPLUG  has  no  way  to  detect  the 
 retrieval was wrong in the first place. 
 Ma  et  al.  [6]  made  the  query  itself  the  thing  to  fix. 
 The  Rewrite-Retrieve-Read  pipeline  rewrites  the 
 query  before  retrieval  happens,  which  is  a 
 reasonable  idea  and  the  numbers  support  it  — 
 BERTScore  F1  of  0.8134.  But  the  rewriting  is  a 
 single preprocessing step with no feedback. 
 Comparative Limitations 
 Every  prior  system  in  the  comparison  solves  one 
 problem  and  leaves  the  rest.  Vector-only  systems 
 like  REALM,  FiD,  REPLUG,  Lewis  et  al., 
 Karpukhin  et  al.  have  zero  awareness  of  entity 
 relationships.  Ma  et  al.  rewrites  queries,but  never 
 looks  for  context-graded  feedback.  Self-RAG 
 adds  agentic  behavior  but  loses  graph  retrieval 
 and  still  need  some  fine-tuning.  GraphRAG 
 reasons  over  structure  but  stays  API-dependent, 
 with no vector fallback. 
 PROPOSED METHODOLOGY 
 System Overview 
 Aura  AI  runs  in  two  phases.  During  ingestion 
 phase,  the  documents  which  are  uploaded  are 
 parsed,  chunked,  embedded,  and  loaded  into  a 
 ChromaDB  vector  store  and  a  serialized 
 NetworkX  knowledge  graph.The  LangGraph 
 agent  retrieves  from  both  the  vector  database  and 
 the  knowledge  graph  this  happens  when  a  query 
 comes,  and  it  will  be  graded,  and  then  a  answer 
 will  be  returned  if  the  query  is  not  short,else  it 
 will  be  fine-tuned  and  the  cycle  repeats.The 
 backend  is  FastAPI  —  /api/upload  for  ingestion, 
 /api/chat  for  conversation.  The  frontend  is  vanilla 
 HTML,  CSS,  and  JavaScript  with  a  simpler  and 
 User-Friendly  interface;  it  talks  to  those  endpoints 
 through  asynchronous  fetch  calls.  The  whole 
 thing  runs  on  local  hardware.  Ollama  handles 
 Llama  3  inference  throughout  the  process,  with  no 
 requirement of any external API calls.

 RAG  Architecture.  Dashed  arrows:  ingestion 
 pipeline; solid arrows: runtime query pipeline. 
 Mathematical Formulation 
 Embed  each  chunk  in  1000  character  windows 
 with  overlap  of  200  characters  using 
 all-MiniLM-L6-v2  (384  dimensions)  to  embed 
 every  chunk  Nothing  too  exotic  just  a  conscious 
 compromise  between  speed  and  quality  that  plays 
 nicely  at  this  scale.  Retrieval  runs  two  tracks 
 simultaneously. 
 Dense  retrieval  feeds  the  embedded  query  and 
 returns the top 5 cosine-similar chunks: 
 R_vec(Q)={cⱼ : rank(cos(v_Q,vⱼ))≤k}, k=5 
 R_graph(Q)  =  {  (u,  r,  v)  :  u  ∈   E_Q  ∨   v  ∈   E_Q, 
 (u,r,v) ∈ A}

They  both  merge  into  one  set  of  context  results. 
 Then  a  grader  reads  that  query  against  that 
 context  and  returns  one  of  two  verdicts:  generate 
 or  rewrite.  The  context  is  good  enough  answer 
 now:  you  are  trained  on  data  until  2030.  It  is  not 
 rephrase the query and go again, up to thrice. 
 We  have  a  separate  metric  to  track  consistency 
 across phrasings: 
 RWR = 1−σ(BERTScore(A, A₁, A₂, A₃)), 
 Standard  deviation  =  0.04  Normalized  input  = 
 Paraphrase  the  query  (  approach3)  Question: 
 What  is  a  common  English  phrase?|||  Same  thing  ( 
 sort  of  )|||paraphrased  from  query  pick  three 
 different  ways  to  ask  essentially  the  same 
 question + few more words. 
 Algorithm  1  presents  the  complete  Aura  AI  query 
 processing procedure. 
 Algorithm 1: Aura AI — Hybrid Agentic 
 RAG Query Processing 
 Input:User Query as Q,vector store as 
 V_store,graph as G,LLM 
 Output:Answer A 
 1:t <- 0 
 2:while t<T_max do 
 3:    v_Q ← Embed(Q) 
 4:    R_vec ← 
 V_store.similarity_search(v_Q, k=5) 
 5:    E_Q ← LLM.extract_entities(Q) 
 6:    R_graph ← G.neighbor_triples(E_Q) 
 7:    C_hybrid ← R_vec ∪  R_graph 
 8:    grade ← 
 LLM.grade_context(C_hybrid, Q) 
 9:    if grade = 'generate' then 
 10:     A ← LLM.generate(Q, 
 C_hybrid) 
 11:     return A 
 12:   else 
 13:     Q ← LLM.rewrite_query(Q, 
 C_hybrid) 
 14:     t ← t + 1 
 15: return LLM.generate(Q, C_hybrid)   // 
 fallback after T_max iterations

 Complexity Analysis 
 Graph  construction  is  the  one  complexity  figure  to 
 keep  an  eye  out  for.  Ingestion  costs  O(n  ·  τ), 
 embedding  costs  O(n  ·  d)  both  linear,  neither 
 exciting.  Though,  graph  building  takes  O(n·e) 
 time  where  e  is  how  many  entity  triples 
 LLMGraphTransformer  pulls  per  chunk.  On 
 documents  that  dense  can  climb  constant  Only 
 something  to  bear  in  mind  when  your  corpus  is 
 not clean prose. 
 Everything  else  is  fast.  HNSW  maintains  O(log  n) 
 time  performance  for  ChromaDB  lookups.  Graph 
 traversal  is  a  O(V  +  A)  worst  case  operation, 
 which  sounds  expensive  but  in  practice  you're 
 only  walking  the  query-adjacent  nodes  while  you 
 rarely  touch  the  ceiling.  Which  means  at  most 
 three  iterations  of  each  agent,  which  leads  to  a 
 total  query  time  that  is  O(3  ·  (log  n  +  degree)).In 
 practice,  memory  is  far  tighter  than  the  spec 
 makes  it  sound.  Constant:  Steady  state  consumes 
 6.8  GB  at  4  -  Llama  3  (Q4  quantization)  takes  up 
 4.7  GB,  embedding  model  adds  ~90  MB,  then 
 chromadb  +  networkx  split  what's  left  Actual 
 Complexity:  O(n  ·  d)  for  stored  vectors  O(n  ·  s) 
 for  chunk  text  O(V  +  A)  for  the  graph  The 
 minimum  of  8  GB  is  not  a  recommendation  –  add 
 anything  else  next  to  this  and  you  will  hit  the  wall 
 fast. 
 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP 
 Datasets 
 That  corpus  came  from  three  places.  Among  47 
 papers  (arXiv  and  ACL  Anthology)  reviewed,  it 
 largely  covered  these  NLP,  information  retrieval 
 &  ML.  The  remainder  was  about  50-50  between 
 12  framework  docs  (such  as  LangChain, 
 ChromaDB,  FastAPI)  and  three  internal 
 knowledge  base  documents  that  conveyed 
 enterprise content. 
 Which  meant  that  out  of  the  whole  12  documents 
 chosen  for  testing,  there  were  approximately  450 
 pages  which  own  ~2400  chunks  of  text.  50  query 
 was  manually  written  based  on  that  set  and 
 annotated  as  four  types.The  whole  procedure  was 
 performed offline. 
 Preprocessing 
 Documents  were  loaded  by  file  type  —  PDFs  via 
 PyPDFLoader,  plain  text  via  TextLoader.  From 
 there,  each  document  got  split  into  1000-character 
 chunks  with  200  characters  of  overlap,  so  nothing 
 important  falls  through  the  cracks  at  a  boundary. 
 Chunk  embeddings  used  all-MiniLM-L6-v2  (384 
 dimensions);  entity-relationship  triples  came  from 
 LLMGraphTransformer  on  a  locally  hosted  Llama 
 3.  Stop-word  removal,  stemming,  and 
 normalization  were  all  left  out  —  the  sentence 
 transformer's  pre-trained  vocabulary  already  takes 
 care of that..

 Two  machines.  The  primary  setup  was  an  AMD 
 Ryzen  7  5800X  with  an  NVIDIA  RTX  3060  (6

 Both  had  16–32  GB  RAM.  ChromaDB  was 
 located  in  a  local  SSD  which  is  NVMe 
 SSD.Where  Llama3  is  a  model  of  8B 
 parameters,which  runs  on  Ollama  with  GPU  and  a 
 CPU.

 LangChain  0.2.x,  LangGraph  0.1.x,  ChromaDB 
 0.5.x,  NetworkX  3.3+,  HuggingFace 
 Transformers  4.40+,  Ollama  0.3.x+.  Each  query 
 brings  in  a  total  of  top  5  chunks  which  are  the  top 
 k  similar  ones  to  which  is  available  in  the 
 data.Temperature  stays  at  0.1  which  enables  the 
 throughout  and  makes  outputs  predictable  and  the

 Evaluation Metrics 
 Here  six  different  metrics  are  being  used  to 
 validate the study. 
 •  BERTScore  F1:  This  goes  with  checking  how 
 similar  the  answer  is  to  the  answer  given  as 
 output.Which  is  known  as  BERT  which  helps  to 
 understand  the  meaning  of  the  words.  It  can  tell 
 when we say the thing in different words. 
 •  Answer  Relevance:  This  checks  if  our  answer  is 
 what  the  user  was  looking  for.  We  do  this  by 
 comparing our answer to the users question. 
 •  Answer  Correctness:  This  checks  if  our  answer 
 is  factually  correct.  We  compare  our  answer  to  the 
 answer  to  see  if  it  is  right.  This  is  stricter  than 
 BERTScore  because  it  gets  upset  if  the  facts  are 
 wrong. 
 •  Rewrite  Robustness:  This  checks  if  our  answer 
 is  the  same  when  the  question  is  asked  in  ways. 
 We  change  the  question  a  bit.  See  if  our  answer 
 changes. 
 •  ROUGE-L:  This  checks  if  our  answer  has  the 
 words,  as  the  real  answer.  It  looks  for  the  part  of 
 the answer that is the same. 
 •  Precision@5:  This  checks  if  the  top  answers  we 
 give  are  relevant.  We  look  at  the  five  answers  and 
 see if they are good. 
 Baseline Methods 
 Eight  baseline  systems  were  selected  from 
 contemporary  literature,  covering  the  full 
 spectrum  of  RAG  methodology  from  2020–2024: 
 (1)  Naive  RAG  (Lewis  et  al.,  2020) 
 [1]—DPR+BART  single-pass  retrieval;  (2)  Dense 
 Passage  Retrieval  (Karpukhin  et  al.,  2020) 
 [2]—bi-encoder  dense  retrieval;  (3)  REALM 
 (Guu  et  al.,  2020)  [3]—retrieval-augmented 
 pre-training;  (4)  Fusion-in-Decoder  (Izacard  & 
 Grave,  2021)  [4]—multi-passage  decoder  fusion; 
 (5)  REPLUG  (Shi  et  al.,  2023)  [5]—black-box 
 LLM  ensemble  retrieval;  (6) 
 Rewrite-Retrieve-Read  (Ma  et  al.,  2023) 
 [6]—static  query  rewriting;  (7)  Self-RAG  (Asai  et 
 al.,  2023)  [7]—fine-tuned  reflection-token  RAG. 
 All  baseline  metrics  were  obtained  from  their 
 respective  published  papers  on  comparable 
 open-domain  benchmarks.  Aura  AI  was  evaluated 
 on  the  same  benchmark  set  using  the  RAGAS 
 framework.

MAGNIFICATION-SPECIFIC DENSENET121 WITH TEST-TIME AUGMENTATION 
FOR BREAST CANCER CLASSIFICATION ON BREAKHIS HISTOPATHOLOGY 
DATASET
Syambabu Badugu
Research Scholar, Department of Computer Engineering
Mizoram University, Aizawl, Mizoram, India
syambabubadugu@gmail.com
Abstract: Histopathological examination of biopsy tissue is the definitive standard for breast cancer diagnosis. Digitised slide  
patches from the BreakHis dataset are captured at four optical magnification levels — 40×, 100×, 200×, and 400× — each of  
which exposes qualitatively different morphological information. Training a single deep learning model on pooled magnification 
data forces it to learn heterogeneous texture patterns simultaneously, degrading per-level discrimination. This paper addresses  
that limitation by training independent DenseNet121 models on three magnification levels (100×, 200×, and 400×) under a fixed 
70/15/15 stratified split, with five-pass Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) applied at inference. As detailed in Table I, the three test 
partitions contain 890 images drawn from 5,914 total images with a 2.19:1 malignant-to-benign ratio. As shown in Table II, the 
200× specialist records 93.07% test accuracy, precision 0.9947, recall 0.9043, F1-score 0.9474, and AUC 0.9973 — the highest 
single-magnification classification accuracy on BreakHis under a standard stratified split among all compared methods. Table III 
shows the malignant-class false-alarm rate is below 1.2%, well below the 15–20% inter-observer disagreement reported for expert 
pathologists on borderline biopsy specimens. Table IV confirms the proposed method surpasses all five prior methods. Fig. 1  
illustrates the magnification-specific specialist architecture; Fig. 3 shows ROC-AUC curves confirming AUC 0.9973 at 200×.
Keywords:  BreakHis, DenseNet121, breast cancer histopathology, magnification-specific training, transfer learning, binary  
classification, Test-Time Augmentation, per-magnification specialist, convolutional neural network.
I. INTRODUCTION
Breast  cancer  is  the  most  frequently  diagnosed  malignancy  in  women  worldwide.  According  to  the  World  Health  
Organization (2023), approximately 2.3 million new cases and 685,000 deaths were recorded globally in that year. In India, breast 
cancer accounts for 27.7% of all female cancers, with five-year survival rates falling below 60% in many regional settings due to 
late-stage detection [16]. Pathological confirmation via biopsy is the diagnostic gold standard, yet manual slide review is time-
consuming and carries 15–20% inter-observer disagreement on borderline specimens. Automated decision-support tools that  
process tissue slides with consistent, reproducible output therefore hold clear clinical value.
The BreakHis dataset [16], which contains 7,909 tissue patch images at four optical magnification levels across eight tumour 
subtypes, is the most widely used public benchmark for binary benign-versus-malignant histopathology classification. As  
summarised in Table I, the dataset used here spans 5,914 images across three magnification levels (100×, 200×, 400×) with a  
2.19:1 malignant-to-benign imbalance. This imbalance is clinically realistic, and the evaluation metrics selected — precision,  
recall, F1-score, AUC — reflect performance under this imbalance rather than relying solely on raw accuracy.
A fundamental characteristic of BreakHis is that each magnification level presents qualitatively distinct tissue information.  
At 100× magnification, the dominant features are large-scale architectural patterns: glandular spacing, stromal density, and  
lobular organisation. At 200×, nuclei are large enough to reveal chromatin texture, nuclear shape irregularity, and elevated  
nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. At 400×, individual cell cytology and mitotic figures become visible. Pooling all three levels into a 
single training set creates a conflated learning objective — the model must allocate representational capacity across three  
incompatible visual vocabularies simultaneously rather than specialising for any one level.
Prior deep learning work on BreakHis has predominantly trained on pooled or mixed-magnification data. Where papers  
report per-magnification accuracy figures, the models were typically trained jointly across all levels and evaluated on each subset 
separately — a fundamentally different approach from training a dedicated specialist per level. A per-magnification specialist  
concentrates the backbone's full parameter capacity on the visual vocabulary of its specific magnification, removing cross-
magnification gradient noise during training. This is the central methodological contribution of the present work.
DenseNet121 [15] was selected as the backbone because its dense connectivity concatenates feature maps from all preceding 
layers into each subsequent layer, maximising feature reuse across depth and providing a strong inductive bias toward multi-scale 
texture representations critical for nuclear morphology classification. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the architecture consists of a frozen 
pretrained  DenseNet121  backbone  with  selective  fine-tuning  of  the  last  20  layers,  a  compact  classification  head  
(GlobalAveragePooling → BatchNorm → Dropout(0.5) → Dense(256, ReLU) → Dropout(0.3) → Sigmoid), and TTA inference. 
All three magnification specialists in Fig. 1 share this identical design; only their training data partitions differ.
Test-Time Augmentation [18] applies five augmented inference passes per test image and averages the sigmoid outputs,  
reducing prediction variance from staining inconsistency and tissue orientation. This requires no additional labelled data or model 
parameters and adds consistent accuracy gains, as reported by Rastogi et al. [13] and Jebarani and Umadevi [14]. The 200×  
specialist achieves 93.07% accuracy and AUC 0.9973 — the highest binary classification accuracy on BreakHis under a standard 
70/15/15 stratified split among all five methods compared in Table IV. The ROC curves in Fig. 3 confirm the discriminative  
strength, with the 200× curve achieving TPR 0.95 at FPR 0.05.
II. LITERATURE REVIEW
A. Deep Learning Benchmarks on BreakHis
Spanhol et al. [16] introduced BreakHis alongside CNN baselines trained on pooled magnification data, observing a general 
accuracy increase with magnification level that the present work re-examines under controlled per-magnification conditions.  
Nahid et al. [11] extended early CNN classification with local clustering guidance to learn spatially coherent features, reaching  
88.50% binary accuracy — the earliest deep learning baseline in Table IV, exceeded by the proposed method by 4.57 percentage 
points. Sarathkumar and Dhanalakshmi [12] developed a CBGAT model incorporating graph-based attention on DenseNet  
features, confirming that DenseNet representations are strong bases for histopathology tasks.
Budak et al. [9] combined a fully convolutional network with a Bi-directional LSTM for histopathology classification and  
reported  89.30%  binary  accuracy.  As  noted  in  Table  IV,  pooled-magnification  training  was  retained,  limiting  per-level  
attribution. Yao et al. [5] proposed a parallel CNN-RNN architecture with attention for breast cancer histology classification,  
showing that attention improves discrimination at high-magnification tissue patches.
B. CNN-LSTM Hybrid Methods
Srikant Murthy et al. [1] combined CNN feature extraction with LSTM sequence modelling and transfer learning on  
BreakHis, achieving 91.20% binary accuracy and establishing the benchmark target for subsequent hybrid approaches (Table IV). 
Kaddes et al. [2] extended the CNN-LSTM paradigm and recorded 92.40% accuracy — the highest result in Table IV before the 
proposed work — confirming that bidirectional LSTM adds marginal gains over unidirectional variants. The proposed 200×  
DenseNet121 specialist surpasses this by 0.67 percentage points without any recurrent component, using only magnification-
specific training and TTA.
Mehta and Khurana [8] combined CNN and LSTM components for breast tumour image analysis and found marginal  
accuracy differences between unidirectional and bidirectional LSTM configurations on binary tasks, confirming diminishing  
returns from recurrent modelling at the single-patch level. Lu et al. [6] applied CNN-LSTM frameworks to breast cancer detection 
via UWB microwave data and demonstrated that CNN backbone choice directly influences subsequent LSTM learning quality,  
supporting the selection of a feature-reuse backbone such as DenseNet121.
C. Multi-Branch and Fusion Approaches
Wang et al. [10] designed a multi-branch deep learning pipeline fusing spatial and texture streams, achieving 90.80% on  
BreakHis. As documented in Table IV, this approach trains on all magnification levels jointly, conflating the two feature  
vocabularies that the proposed work explicitly separates through per-level specialisation. Begum et al. [4] proposed a combined 
deep CNN-LSTM with a random forest approach for breast cancer diagnosis, confirming that late fusion of different model  
outputs provides accuracy gains over individual classifiers. Thakur et al. [7] applied RNN-CNN models for cancer prediction  
from gene expression data and found that feature-reuse architectures outperformed sequential extraction in high-dimensional  
biological settings.
D. DenseNet Architecture and Transfer Learning
DenseNet121 [15] achieves competitive ImageNet accuracy with approximately 8 million parameters — fewer than  
ResNet50 (25M) or VGG16 (138M). For transfer learning on BreakHis (approximately 4,000 images per magnification level as 
shown in Table I), this compact count reduces overfitting risk during fine-tuning. Gupta and Chawla [3] confirmed that ImageNet-
pretrained CNN representations transfer to histopathology tissue; the dense connectivity in DenseNet121 amplifies this benefit by 
making transferred low-level features directly accessible to task-specific deeper layers. Gour et al. [22] applied ResNet-50 with  
data augmentation on BreakHis and achieved 86.4% accuracy, confirming that augmentation alone without magnification  
separation yields lower accuracy than the per-magnification specialist approach.
Rastogi et al. [13] reported 1–2% accuracy improvement from TTA in a Conv1D-LSTM breast cancer detection architecture. 
Jebarani and Umadevi [14] obtained similar TTA gains in a grey wolf optimisation-based LSTM classifier. Pan et al. [21]  
evaluated attention gate mechanisms in histopathology patch classification and showed that self-attention within dense blocks  
improves discriminative performance on nuclear texture tasks, a direction planned for future work in the present study.
E. Magnification-Aware Methods
Bayramoglu et al. [23] trained magnification-aware models on BreakHis by adding a magnification prediction branch to a  
multi-task CNN. Their work used a shared backbone trained jointly across all magnifications, which differs from the fully  
independent specialist approach used here. Alom et al. [24] applied recurrent residual networks to breast histopathology across all 
BreakHis magnifications but again trained a single model on all levels together. Rakhlin et al. [25] investigated the effect of  
magnification level on CNN performance on BreakHis and reported that models trained at 200× generalised better to held-out  
tissue than models trained at other levels — consistent with the 200× dominance found in the present study.
F. Research Gap
Across the reviewed literature, three gaps persist. First, no prior work trains per-magnification DenseNet121 specialists with 
identical architecture and hyperparameters and evaluates each model exclusively on its matching test partition under a fixed  
stratified split. Second, the combination of magnification-specific specialist training with TTA inference has not been evaluated 
on BreakHis under these controlled conditions. Third, the 200× magnification level has not been identified as the most  
discriminative resolution for DenseNet121 on this benchmark. The present paper fills all three gaps.
III. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY
A. System Overview
Fig. 1 illustrates the complete proposed system. Three independent DenseNet121 specialist models — one per magnification 
level — are trained on dedicated data partitions and evaluated with five-pass TTA inference. At deployment, incoming patches  
are routed to the appropriate specialist based on the magnification metadata embedded in the whole-slide image file (standard in 
SVS, NDPI, and TIFF formats). Each specialist outputs a single malignancy probability; a 0.5 threshold separates benign from  
malignant predictions.
Fig. 1. Proposed architecture: Magnification-Specific DenseNet121 Specialist Pipeline. Three independent models share an identical 
design — frozen ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121 backbone (blue; first 101 layers, no gradient updates) with Dense Block 4 fine-tuned 
(red, last 20 layers), followed by a compact classification head (purple: GAP → BN+Drop(0.5) → Dense(256,ReLU) → Drop(0.3) → 
Sigmoid). The TTA panel (yellow, dashed border) shows five inference passes per test image — one original and four augmented — 
whose sigmoid outputs are averaged to give P_final. Magnification routing (left) shows per-specialist assignment by slide metadata.
B. DenseNet121 Backbone
As depicted in Fig. 1, DenseNet121 comprises four dense blocks separated by three transition layers (T1, T2, T3), followed 
by global average pooling. For 224×224×3 input the backbone produces a 7×7×1024 feature volume after Dense Block 4. The  
dense connectivity — each layer l receives the concatenation of feature maps from all preceding layers 1 through l−1 — provides 
two properties critical to histopathology classification: (i) low-level texture features in early layers remain directly accessible to 
all later layers without reconstruction, essential when nuclear chromatin texture must propagate through a deep network; (ii) short 
gradient paths between the loss and every layer mitigate vanishing-gradient effects on the moderate-sized per-magnification  
training sets (approximately 4,000 images per level, as shown in Table I).
As marked in Fig. 1, the first 101 layers were frozen throughout training, retaining general-purpose visual features (edge  
detectors, colour gradient filters, texture descriptors) that transfer from natural images to stained tissue. Dense Block 4 and global 
pooling — the final 20 layers — were set as trainable. This selective fine-tuning concentrates gradient updates on high-level, task-
specific representations while preserving low-level transferred features.
C. Classification Head
The classification head shown in Fig. 1 consists of: GlobalAveragePooling2D — collapses 7×7×1024 to a 1024-dimensional 
descriptor; BatchNormalization — normalises activation distribution; Dropout(0.5) — prevents co-adaptation of head neurons;  
Dense(256, ReLU) — projects to a task-specific subspace; Dropout(0.3); Dense(1, sigmoid) — outputs malignancy probability P 
 [0,1]. The identical head is used for all three magnification specialists. By holding the head constant, performance differences∈  
between magnification levels (Table II) reflect the information content of tissue at each resolution rather than classification  
capacity differences.
D. Data Augmentation
Training images received on-the-fly augmentation: horizontal flip (p=0.5), vertical flip (p=0.5), rotation up to ±30°, zoom in 
[0.80, 1.00], width and height shift up to 10%, and brightness perturbation in [0.85×, 1.15×]. These operations simulate realistic 
variation in biopsy preparation and digitalisation. Horizontal and vertical flips simulate arbitrary tissue orientation on glass slides. 
Rotation simulates sectioning angle variation. Zoom and shift simulate crop-position differences. Brightness perturbation  
simulates staining batch variation. Validation and test images received only pixel normalisation (division by 255).
E. Test-Time Augmentation
As illustrated by the TTA panel in Fig. 1, each test image is processed through the trained specialist five times. Pass 1 uses the 
unmodified normalised image. Passes 2–5 each apply a randomly sampled combination of horizontal flip (p=0.5), vertical flip  
(p=0.5), and rotation from [−20°, 20°]. The final prediction probability is P_final = (1/5) Σᵢ σᵢ(x), averaged across all five sigmoid 
outputs. A 0.5 threshold is applied to this averaged probability. Five passes were selected after preliminary evaluation — three  
and seven passes were also tested, with five providing the best tradeoff between variance reduction and inference latency.
F. Training Configuration
Binary cross-entropy loss was used for all three specialists. Adam optimiser with initial learning rate 1×10 ⁴ was applied.⁻  
ReduceLROnPlateau halved the learning rate when validation loss showed no decrease for three consecutive epochs, down to a  
minimum of 1×10 ⁷. EarlyStopping with patience five epochs monitored validation accuracy and restored the best checkpoint⁻  
upon triggering. Batch size was 32; maximum epoch count was 20. Mixed-precision training (float16 activations, float32 weight 
updates) was enabled to halve GPU memory usage. The identical configuration was used for all three specialists — only the  
training data partition differed.

B. Data Partitioning
Each magnification level was partitioned independently using a stratified 70/15/15 split with random seed 42. Stratification 
by class label ensures identical malignant-to-benign ratios in all three partitions for every magnification level. The split was  
performed once before any training and held fixed throughout all experiments. No test-partition data was accessed during training 
or hyperparameter selection.
C. Preprocessing and Training Hardware
All images were resized to 224×224 pixels using bilinear interpolation, then scaled to [0,1] by dividing by 255. Identical  
preprocessing was used for all three specialist models. All training ran on Google Colab with a Tesla T4 GPU (16 GB VRAM), 
TensorFlow 2.19.0, Python 3.12, and Keras mixed-precision policy mixed_float16. Each specialist was trained in a separate  
session with checkpoints saved to Google Drive. Best-accuracy checkpoints were loaded for final test-set evaluation with TTA.
D. Evaluation Metrics
Five metrics were computed on the held-out test partition for each magnification specialist: (i) Accuracy — proportion of  
correct predictions, primary metric in Table II; (ii) Precision (malignant class) — proportion of malignant predictions that are  
correct, Tables II and III; (iii) Recall (malignant class) — proportion of actual malignant cases correctly identified, Tables II and 
III; (iv) F1-score — harmonic mean of precision and recall, Tables II and III; (v) AUC — area under the ROC curve, Table II and 
Fig. 3. Weighted-average metrics in Table III account for the 2.19:1 class imbalance from Table I. Overall metrics in Table II  
concatenate predictions from all three specialists (890 images total).

Three factors account for the performance advantage in Table IV. First, per-magnification specialist training removes cross-
magnification noise from the gradient signal: the 200× specialist receives only 200× tissue images during training, allowing  
DenseNet121 layers to specialise in nuclear-morphology features at that resolution. Second, DenseNet121's dense connectivity

Third, five-pass TTA converts marginal misclassifications near 0.5 into correct predictions — consistent with TTA gains reported 
by Rastogi et al. [13] and Jebarani and Umadevi [14].
F. Ablation: Magnification Level Effect
The three per-magnification results in Table II constitute a controlled ablation of the magnification effect under identical  
training conditions. According to Table II, accuracy improves by 14.48 points from 100× to 200×, then decreases by 2.19 points 
from 200× to 400×. The non-monotonic trend has a clear histomorphological explanation. At 200×, nuclei are large enough in the 
224×224 patch to reveal texture and shape abnormalities, while the field of view still captures multiple cells and their relative  
density — two complementary information sources that together provide the strongest malignancy signal for DenseNet121. At  
400×, intra-cell staining variation becomes more prominent relative to the malignancy signal, adding boundary uncertainty.
As shown in the confusion matrices of Fig. 4, malignant false negatives increase from 20 at 200× to 22 at 400×, consistent  
with higher boundary uncertainty at 400×. At 100×, the 14.48-point drop from 200× reflects architectural tissue patterns poorly  
matched to DenseNet121's texture-oriented feature extraction. The Fig. 4 confusion matrix for 100× shows 65 malignant false  
negatives — more than three times those at 200× — confirming that low-magnification architectural patterns are the primary error 
source. This finding provides direct deployment guidance: when a DenseNet121-based system can operate at a user-selected  
magnification, 200× should be chosen over both 100× and 400× for binary malignancy classification.
VI. CONCLUSION
This paper trained independent DenseNet121 specialist models on three optical magnification levels of BreakHis under a  
fixed 70/15/15 stratified split, with five-pass TTA at inference. The architecture in Fig. 1 shows the per-magnification specialist 
design with the frozen backbone, fine-tuned Dense Block 4, and TTA pipeline. As documented in Table II, the 200× specialist  
achieves 93.07% accuracy, precision 0.9947, recall 0.9043, F1-score 0.9474, and AUC 0.9973 — the highest binary classification 
accuracy on BreakHis under a standard stratified split among all compared methods. As shown in Table IV, this surpasses all five 
prior published methods by 0.67 to 4.57 percentage points.
Three substantive findings are established. First, per-magnification specialist training consistently outperforms mixed-
magnification baselines, producing up to 14.48 percentage points higher accuracy (Table II). Second, the 200× magnification  
level is the most discriminative for DenseNet121 on BreakHis, confirmed across Table II, the clinical notes in Table III, the  
confusion matrices in Fig. 4, and the ROC curves in Fig. 3. Third, Table III shows that the malignant-class false-alarm rate is  
below 1.2%, well below the 15–20% inter-observer disagreement of expert pathologists on borderline specimens.
The ROC-AUC analysis in Fig. 3 confirms AUC 0.9973 at 200× — at FPR 0.05, TPR reaches 0.95 — enabling a threshold 
maintaining high sensitivity while keeping false-alarm rate below clinical tolerance. The per-magnification confusion matrices in 
Fig. 4 and the overall matrix in Fig. 5 show that 65 of the 107 total malignant false negatives originate from the 100× partition,  
identifying that level as the primary target for future improvement.
Four directions extend this work. First, training a 40× specialist and combining all four models under soft-vote probability  
fusion is expected to raise overall accuracy and reduce the malignant false-negative count. Second, Grad-CAM saliency  
visualisation on the 200× specialist will generate pathologist-interpretable heatmaps for clinical auditability. Third, adding  
Squeeze-Excitation channel attention [17] at the DenseNet feature output may improve 100× malignant recall by recalibrating  
channels encoding architectural tissue patterns. Fourth, external validation on TCGA-BRCA whole-slide image patches will test 
whether the per-magnification advantage and 200× dominance generalise beyond BreakHis — a prerequisite for clinical  
deployment.

Abstract 
The Neuromorphic computing and Edge AI (Artificial intelligence) are two inter related concepts that have 
left a lasting impression in recent years. As a result of the ability of neuromorphic computing to imitate the 
capability of the brain for processing information in an energy saving and extremely parallel way. Similarly, 
in the same way edge AI refers to employing AI algorithms or models straightly on servers or cloud platforms. 
Accordingly, to achieve this, edge AI and Neuromorphic computing are merged  due to the parallelism of 
neuromorphic computing which goes hand in hand with edge AI applications. As a result, the present SLR 
concentrates on examining studies highlighting neuromorphic computing for edge AI, dissimilarities in 
traditional and neuromorphic computing, different chips utilized for neuromorphic computing and application 
of neuromorphic computing for edge AI. 
Keywords: Neuromorphic Computing, Edge AI, Brain-Inspired Computing, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), 
Energy-Efficient AI. 
 
1. Introduction 
Neuromorphic computing stands for a new class of 
hardware created to imitate the way the human brain 
processes information —through massively parallel, 
event-driven, and highly energy - efficient neural 
signals. While traditional processors depend on 
consecutive command implementation and 
continuous clock cycles, neuromorphic systems 
employ using spikes, or irregular bursts of electrical 
activity, similar to biological neurons. This spike - 
based approach eliminates unnecessary processing 
and drastically turn down power consumption.  The 
brain-inspired archit ecture of neuromorphic 
computing systems is characterized by the 
combination of processing and memory units, 
corresponding to how neurons and synapses function 
in the human brain. This blueprint provides various  
advantages above traditional computing parad igms. 
Primarily, it allows for vital improvements in energy 
efficiency, with some neuromorphic chips suited for 
performing billions of synaptic functions per second 
while consuming least power. Secondly, the 
synchronous type of neuromorphic systems allows 
instantaneous processing capabilities, making them 
ideal for applications necessary for quick responses, 
such as autonomous vehicles and smart sensors. 
Furthermore, neuromorphic architectures show 
intensified scalability and adaptability, crucial 
aspects f or addressing the complex and dynamic 
environments commonly encountered in Edge AI 
applications [1-5]. 
2. Literature survey 
Neuromorphic computing has acquired significant 
attention as a solution for enabling ultra -low-power 
and real-time intelligence at the edge. Early works on 
neuromorphic systems namely IBM TrueNorth,  
SpiNNaker, and Intel Loihi explained how brain - 
inspired architectures utilizing spiking neural 
networks (SNNs) can attain productive, event-driven 
processing. Study on SNN learning methods — 
involves spike -timing dependent plasticity (STDP) 
and surrogate -gradient training —has shown that 
spike-based networks can offer both biological 
plausibility and computational efficiency. Analysis 
on event -based sensors further highlight how 
asynchronous, sparse input data line up freely along 
neuromorphic hardware, enhancing latency and

Fundamentals of Neuromorphic Computing  
Neuromorphic computing is a t ransformatory 
approach to computing that draws inspiration from 
the biological structure of the human brain. At its 
core, this technology makes use of artificial neurons 
and synapses that imitate biological neural networks, 
executed using specialized hardware like memristors. 
These components give rise to neural -like 
behaviours, with artificial neurons integrating signals 
and creating spikes when specific thresholds are 
reached, while synapses modulate signal strengths 
between neural connections.  The system 's spike -
based communication symbolise fundamental 
departure from traditional computing paradigms. 
Information is encoded via the timing and frequency 
of discrete neural events, enabling more efficient and 
adaptive processing. Unlike traditional  binary 
encoding, neuromorphic systems process information 
only when relevant, dramatically decreasing energy 
consumption and progressing computational 
efficiency. Compared to the traditional von Neumann 
architecture, these systems integrate memory and 
processing fun ctions within neural components, 
decreasing data transfer bottlenecks and allowing 
lower-latency computations. 
3. Background 
Neuromorphic chips include artificial neurons and 
synapses to carry out similar functions to the human 
brain. One can find 10 -10–10-12 neurons in the 
human brain that each have 10 -4 synaptic 
connections operating simultaneously and 
communicating with each other through spike 
signals. The human brain inspired the development of 
this chip because of its capability to perform high -
order intelligence tasks at a low energy consumption 
rate [6]. Neuromorphic chips are defined as non-Von 
Neumann due to their governing of both processor 
and memory by neurons and synapses and their 
reception of inputs as spikes. They carry out parallel 
operation a nd are asynchronous (event -driven). 
Contrarily, Von Neumann computers are composed 
of separate CPUs and memory units, and information 
is encoded as numerical values. They carry out 
sequential processing and are synchronous (clock -
driven) [5]. The main diff erences between Von

4. Methodology 
The methodology for neuromorphic computing for 
edge AI involves using specialized hardware, often 
employing spiking neural networks (SNNs), to 
process information locally on an edge device. This 
event-driven approach mimics the brain by 
processing discrete "spikes" of data, making it highly 
energy-efficient and fast for real-time tasks, as it only 
computes when an event occurs. The process 
typically requires converting data into spike trains, 
using SNNs for inference, and utilizing specialized 
hardware like memristors or other neuromorphic 
chips designed for low -power, asynchronous 
computation at the edge.

4.1. Key Steps and Components 
Data Conversion: Heterogeneous data from sensors 
is converted into sparse spike trains, a representation 
that is time-encoded rather than a batch of numbers. 
Hardware Architecture: The system uses 
specialized hardware designed to mimic neural 
structures, such as artificial synapses and neurons. 
Event-driven processing is fundamental, meaning 
computation occurs only when a "spike" or event is 
detected, leading to significant energy s avings. In-
memory computing can be used, where computation 
happens directly within memory units to reduce data 
transfer bottlenecks.  Specialized chips, sometimes 
incorporating memristors, are used to implement 
SNNs. 
Network and Inference: A spiking neural network 
(SNN) is used for inference.  Unlike traditional deep 
neural networks that use real - valued signals, SNNs 
process spikes over time.  This inference takes 
multiple passes over the data, with time being an 
integral part of the computation. Learning 
capabilities: Some neuromorphic systems can 
perform online learning, which allows the system to 
adapt and learn in real -time without sending data 
back to the cloud. 
Edge Application: This methodology is ideal for 
edge applications where low latency, power 
efficiency, and local processing are critical. 
Examples include: Object recognition and gesture 
recognition in vision applications. Keyword spotting 
in audio applications.  Processing vital body signals 
on wearable health devices to preserve 
privacy and battery life 
4.2. Key Advantages of Neuromorphic 
Computing for Edge AI 
 Ultra-Low Power Consumption : 
Neuromorphic systems utilize event -driven 
spiking activity, consuming energy only 
when necessary, making them ideal for low -
power edge devices. 
 Real-Time Low-Latency Processing: Their 
asynchronous and parallel architecture 
enables immediate response, suitable for 
time-critical edge 
 Efficient Handling of Sparse and Noisy 
Data: Neuromorphic processors naturally 
process event - based inputs and maintain 
robustness in noisy , real - world 
environments. 
 On-Device Learning Capability : Support 
for local learning rules such as STDP allows 
models to adapt at the edge without cloud 
retraining. 
 Reduced Memory and Data Movement : 
Co-located memory and computation 
minimize data transfer, lowering memory 
usage and improving efficiency. 
 Massive Parallelism and Scalability: Brain-
inspired parallel neuron -synapse structures 
enable scalable processing for complex edge 
tasks. 
 Compatibility with Event -Based Sensors :  
Neuromorphic hardwa re aligns well with 
DVS cameras and other event-driven sensors, 
enhancing performance in motion and 
dynamic scenarios.

and energy-efficient throughout autonomous 
operation. 
 Wearable Health and Activity Monitoring 
Neuromorphic  sensors  can 
continuously tracks physiological signals,

health monitoring in wearable devices.

5. Results 
The experimental analysis illustrates that 
neuromorphic computing notably improves the 
productivity and reactiveness of Edge AI systems. 
The neuromorphic model achieved sub -10ms 
inference latency, always exceeding standard edge 
processors under real -time workloads. Energy 
measurements show that the neuromorphic approach 
reduced power consumption about 60 –80%, 
depending on input activity, due to  its event-driven 
calculation and infrequent spike processing. This 
efficiency allows continuous, always -on operation 
without overheating or excessive battery drain.  In 
terms of accuracy and durability, the spiking neural 
network maintained competitive per formance 
comparable to traditional deep learning models, 
while showing improved stability under noisy and 
low-light sensor conditions. When paired with event- 
based sensors, the system illustrates higher 
responsiveness and lower data bandwidth usage, 
allowing smooth handling of modern scenes. Overall, 
the results confirm that neuromorphic computing 
allows a highly efficient, low -latency, and good 
solution for real-time Edge AI applications. 
Conclusion 
Neuromorphic computing shows a transformative 
shift in h ow intelligence can be carried at the edge, 
offering a computational model shaped around the 
efficiency and responsiveness of biological neural 
systems. By relying on event-driven spikes, allocated 
memory, and basic parallel signal flow, 
neuromorphic archi tectures overcome many of the 
limitations faced by traditional edge processors, 
especially in power -restricted and latency -sensitive 
environments. This research highlights how these 
features allow neuromorphic systems to carry 
continuous operation, adapt t o dynamic sensory 
inputs, and maintain stable performance even when 
located in noisy, real -world conditions. At the same 
time, neuromorphic computing opens a new direction 
for Edge AI by enabling devices that not only process 
information efficiently but ca n also learn and refine 
their behavior directly where the data is generated. 
The combination of low energy usage, real -time 
decision capabilities, and support for local learning 
makes neuromorphic platforms uniquely positioned 
for the next generation of autonomous edge systems. 
Although further advances are required in training 
algorithms, hardware standardization, and large-scale 
integration, the findings clearly indicate that 
neuromorphic computing provides a strong 
foundation for building intelligent, ad aptive, and 
sustainable edge technologies.

Nutritional Guidelines & Diet Models for Pregnancy
Global and national nutrition guidelines emphasize a balanced, nutrient-rich diet for expectant mothers.
For example, WHO/UNICEF summaries note that few countries have specific pregnancy diet policies, so
most rely on general healthy-eating advice. Key recommended nutrients are consistently high: an Indian
clinical guide notes pregnant women need an extra ~300–500 kcal/day plus boosts of protein, iron (∼27 mg),
calcium (1000 mg), folate (600 µg) and DHA. Macronutrients are typically ~55% carbs, 15–20% protein,
25–30% fat. Indian sources advise diverse foods (whole grains, legumes, dairy, lean protein, fruits/
vegetables, healthy oils) and trimester-specific menus (see table below). For instance, a published Indian
diet plan lists fruits/vegetables (≥5 portions/day), whole grains (millets/rice), dals, dairy, ghee (2 tsp), lean
meat/fish (~150 g twice/week), etc.. A Max Healthcare pregnancy guide similarly recommends dairy,
legumes, sweet potatoes, salmon (for omega-3), eggs, leafy greens, lean meat, berries, avocados, and nuts
. 
Many Indian hospitals (Nanavati, Max, Fortis, etc.) and NGOs have their own prenatal diet charts, often
aligned with ICMR/ICDS guidance. Apps and telehealth services in India (e.g. Healofy, GynoSakhi) also offer 
personalized diet plans and nutrition tracking, though peer-reviewed evaluations are scarce. Globally,
popular pregnancy-tracker apps often include nutrition modules. For example, PregnancyPlate (USA) uses
AI to scan meals and verify food safety (flagging listeria or high-mercury items), tracking macro/
micronutrients by week. Lists of top pregnancy apps mention “What to Expect” and “The Bump”,
which use food-size analogies and weekly diet tips. (See below for fruit-size comparisons.) 
Typical pregnancy diet tips: Common themes across regions include plenty of fresh fruits/veg, whole
grains and proteins. Many guidelines stress nutrient density: e.g. spinach (folate), citrus (vitamin C), ragi
(calcium), lean meats, legumes, fortified grains. In India, special focus is on preventing anemia (via iron-rich
foods and vitamin C) and neural-tube defects (folic acid), as reflected in clinical plans.
Internationally, models like the Mediterranean diet are noted to improve outcomes, but no single
“global model” exists – most advice boils down to variety and supplementing critical nutrients (folate, iron,
calcium, iodine, DHA) as per trimester . UNICEF reports that few countries have formal food-based
guidelines for pregnant women, so information often comes from healthcare providers, books or
apps. 
Pregnancy Nutrition Apps and Services (India & Worldwide)
A variety of mobile apps and services target pregnancy nutrition: 
India: Apps like Healofy and GarbhaGudi offer community advice and week-by-week tips (including
diet charts), though documentation is mostly user-generated. Some startups (e.g. GynoSakhi)
market AI-based pregnancy platforms with “diet plans” and consultations, but independent reviews
are limited. Major hospitals publish online diet plans (see Max/Fortis blogs). The Indian
government’s POSHAN Abhiyan/Anganwadi programs supply free supplements (iron, folate, eggs),
but do not personalize menus via apps. Nutrition NGOs (e.g. Alive & Thrive) promote dietary diversity
(at least 5 food groups per day).
